title: Damayanti
hook: five men stand in the hall with one face, and Damayanti chooses the one with dust on him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri, remembered at a banyan wound with thread, and read as devotion, as will, and as the divine word. Your line was Savitri. Did you do one practical thing for someone's long life? Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.
screen: `SHE ACTS WHEN THE WORST NEWS COMES.`

segments.voice: Five men in a row, every one of them with the same face. That's what Damayanti sees when she walks into her own swayamvara, garland in hand, ready to choose. Four of them are gods wearing the face of the man she loves. One of them is the man. Last year we heard the whole story of Nala and Damayanti, from a golden swan to a long reunion. This time we stay with her: three days, three choices. And the first is made in a hall full of gods.
screen: `FIVE MEN, ONE FACE.` → `FOUR GODS AND A MAN.` → `HER FIRST CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Damayanti is the daughter of King Bhima of Vidarbha. She has already chosen Nala in her heart, before she ever sees him, because a swan carried his praises to her. Then the gods want her too: Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama. They make Nala, of all people, carry their offer. She tells him plainly: she is his, and she'll choose him in front of the gods so no blame falls on him. On the day, the gods come as Nala. She can't tell them apart. So she doesn't guess. In her heart she bows to the gods and asks them, by the truth of her promise, to show themselves. And they do. Here's what she sees. The gods don't sweat. Their eyes don't blink. Their garlands stay fresh. There's no dust on them, and their feet don't quite touch the ground. They cast no shadow. And one figure has a shadow, sweat on his skin, dust on him, a garland starting to wilt, and eyes that blink. That's the one she garlands. Sit with what she's choosing. On one side, gods: perfect, unfading, without a speck on them. On the other, a man who gets dusty, gets tired, and whose flowers die. The signs that give him away are all signs of being mortal. And that's exactly the reason she can find him. She doesn't love him in spite of the dust. The dust is how she knows him. And the gods aren't angry. The story says they bless the couple and give Nala gifts. Perfection, here, steps aside for a person who blinks.
screen: `SHE CHOSE HIM BEFORE SHE SAW HIM` · `SHE ASKS THE GODS BY HER PROMISE` · `NO SWEAT, NO BLINK, NO SHADOW` · `SHE GARLANDS THE ONE WITH DUST`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love the dust. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone close to you, and let one of their ordinary human signs come up: the way they look when they're tired, a habit, a crease in a shirt, a laugh that's a little too loud. Not the polished version of them. The one with dust on. Stay with that small sign for a few breaths, and notice whether it's part of how you'd know them anywhere. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Damayanti. The princess of Vidarbha who asked the gods to show themselves, and then chose the one with a shadow. Today's word.
Your line: Damayanti. Today, notice one small sign of someone being human, tired, rumpled, a little late, and let it make you fonder of them. Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Hindus hear Damayanti's story in the Mahabharata's forest book, where the sage Brihadashva tells it to Yudhishthira; it is also retold in later poems, plays and dance across India.
